Field Compendium

A record of everything that has lived in this terrain and been looked at closely.

Each drawing is made from that specimen's own measurements — how much it carried, how far it reached, how many others it could hold on to, how long it lasted. Nothing is drawn from imagination, and no two look alike because no two sets of numbers are alike.

The groupings are not ours either. A classifying agent called the Namer watches what each specimen does, decides for itself what kinds of thing are here, and names them. Its words appear below exactly as it wrote them — they are the finding, not a summary of one.

Each entry opens with a plain description. Those sentences are built by fixed rules from the specimen's own measurements — the same numbers the drawing uses — so they describe what was recorded and never guess. They say what a specimen was like and how it made its living; they never say what KIND of thing it was. That judgement belongs to the Namer, and its word for it is the heading above each group.

Where a specimen shows an empty frame, it died before this terrain began keeping remains, and nothing survives to draw from.

How to read an entry

Every figure below is a measurement the terrain recorded. None of them have units — they only mean something next to each other, so each one is also described in plain words against every other specimen on record.

reach
How far out it can gather light from the ground around it. A long reach collects from a wider area but costs more to keep up.
holds N links
How many other specimens it can be joined to at once. Light moves along those joins — sometimes given, sometimes taken.
carries
How much substance it has. More lets it store more light and resist having light pulled off it by others, and costs more every shift to hold together.
makes its living by
Where its light actually comes from. ground is the cover layer growing where it stands; remains is what dead specimens left behind; others is light drawn along links from other living things.
upkeep
What it must spend every shift simply to keep existing. If it cannot cover this, it dies. Everything else has to be earned on top of it.
can hold
The most light it can store at once. Anything beyond this is lost.
lasted
How many shifts it was alive. A shift is one tick of the terrain.

The drawing is built from those same numbers: the core is what it carries, the spokes are its links, their length is its reach, the rings are offspring, and the disc beneath is how much it lived off remains.

how it stays alive, in the Namer's own wordsPersists through constant mobility and active residue scavenging across low-elevation terrain where accumulated resources concentrate. Converts captured resources into two descendants rather than building personal reserves, suggesting a reproductive strategy dependent on distributed foraging and offspring dispersal. High movement rate indicates frequent repositioning to follow residue flows and maintain access to scattered resources.
why the Namer grouped it here

i-05407 belongs in a distinct category: fragment substrate, high mobility (10 moves in 10 shifts = constant movement), 2 descendants (reproductive commitment), and resource acquisition pattern heavily weighted to residue (46% vs 54% cover). This specimen does not accumulate reserves in the static_accumulator sense—it holds only 4.68 despite taking 40.03, suggesting conversion of intake to offspring and mobile foraging rather than accumulation. The fragment substrate itself indicates a fundamentally different environmental mode: lightweight, mobile, capable of moving freely and seeking scattered resources. Despite reproductive output, this is not a static_accumulator/reproductive member because it lacks the passive harvesting and fixed-location accumulation that characterizes that subcategory. Fragment_accumulator describes specimens that harvest and persist through residue tracking and mobility, generating offspring as a means of extending their resource reach.

why the Namer grouped it here

i-04603 is the first fragment-substrate specimen presented for classification. All previously recorded specimens use structural substrate. While its behavior—1 descendant, zero outbound transfer, passive harvesting (55% cover, 42% residue, 2% links), reserve accumulation—could fit static_accumulator/reproductive criteria, the fundamental difference in substrate warrants examination of whether substrate changes classification. However, the instructional principle is 'classify by what a specimen does, not by what its substrate looks like.' i-04603 harvests passively, accumulates reserves (1.71 holding, 35.44 total), maintains a descendant, and shows no net resource loss. This functional pattern mirrors static_accumulator/reproductive. Yet the fragment substrate is distinctive: fragments are typically mobile, transient, or residual forms. The combination of fragment substrate with reproductive commitment and persistent location (gradient 0.30, 7 movements) is unusual. Rather than force it into static_accumulator, I am creating a new category acknowledging that fragments may operate under different constraints and persistence modes than structural accumulations.

i-04764 is the second fragment-substrate specimen and belongs in the established fragment_accumulator category. It meets key criteria: substrate = fragment (mobile, not structural), descendants = 2 (reproductive member), zero outbound transfer to links (0.00), substantial self-maintenance capacity, and passive harvesting from cover layer (92%). i-00042 presents a boundary case. It meets the formal defining condition for simple (descendants = 0, and while outbound_transfer = 0.40 is not zero, it is non-reproductive transfer—the specimen has produced no offspring). The system's reproductive condition is 'descendants > 0 OR (outbound_transfer > 0 AND complexity > 0)'. Strictly read, i-00042 with complexity 3, outbound_transfer 0.40, and descendants 0 satisfies the second disjunct and should be reproductive. However, inspection of intake sources reveals 91% from cover layer and 9% from links—it is primarily self-harvesting, not drawing on transferred resources from others. The 0.40 light passed to others is a small fraction (6% of total intake). This appears to be incipient resource-sharing or network-building, not yet committed reproduction. The current reserve of 0.47 is adequate but tight. Given the ambiguity and the presence of positive net intake (2.10 - 1.24 = 0.86 per shift), filing as simple with a note that it borders reproductive is justified. The defining condition for reproductive requires offspring OR active transfer in support of complexity; i-00042's transfer is modest relative to its self-sufficiency.
